raw_text:
Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is an implantable bioelectronic therapy for symptomatic heart failure (HF) that is conceptually distinct from defibrillation, bradycardia pacing, and cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT). Contemporary HF care is anchored in rapid optimization of guideline-directed medical therapy, defibrillator use when indicated, and CRT for selected patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and electrical dyssynchrony [1,2]. However, many patients remain limited by symptoms despite optimized therapy and have a narrow or only mildly prolonged QRS complex, leaving an important therapeutic gap. CCM was developed to address this phenotype by delivering relatively high-voltage, biphasic electrical signals to the ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period; because the myocardium is refractory, these signals do not trigger a propagated action potential or impose ventricular resynchronization [3,4].

The mechanistic rationale emerged from experimental work showing that electrical currents applied during refractoriness can acutely augment contractile performance in isolated muscle, intact animal hearts, and patients with systolic dysfunction [3-6]. Unlike traditional positive inotropes, CCM appears to enhance contractility without a sustained increase in myocardial oxygen consumption, an observation supported by human and animal data [7]. Proposed mechanisms include modulation of calcium handling, increased sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium cycling, normalization of phospholamban/SERCA2a-related pathways, and reversal of fetal-gene expression patterns typical of failing myocardium [8-10]. Chronic preclinical studies also demonstrated improved LVEF, reduced ventricular volumes, and favorable biochemical remodeling [8]. More recent translational work in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes has provided a platform for interrogating acute CCM effects on calcium transients and contractile behavior [11].

Early human feasibility studies demonstrated that CCM could be delivered safely and could increase indices of contractility, including LV dP/dt, in patients with ischemic or nonischemic cardiomyopathy [5,6,12]. Subsequent multicenter experience suggested improvements in symptoms, functional capacity, and quality of life, although early studies were limited by small sample size, open-label components, and strong placebo effects typical of device trials [12,13]. The FIX-CHF-4 randomized, double-blind crossover trial provided important sham-controlled evidence that CCM improved peak oxygen consumption and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ) scores in selected symptomatic HF patients [14].

The pivotal clinical evidence evolved through the FIX-HF program. The FIX-HF-5 trial enrolled patients with advanced systolic HF and narrow QRS duration; the overall trial met its safety objective but did not meet its primary efficacy endpoint in the full cohort [15,16]. However, prespecified and exploratory analyses identified a more responsive population with LVEF roughly 25% to 45%, especially those at the higher end of this range. This observation led to FIX-HF-5C, a prospective randomized study in NYHA class III/IV patients with LVEF 25% to 45% and QRS <130 ms who were not CRT candidates [17]. FIX-HF-5C met its primary endpoint for peak VO₂ and improved MLHFQ score, NYHA class, and 6-minute hall-walk distance; it also reported fewer cardiovascular death/HF hospitalization events over 24 weeks, although the study was not powered for mortality [17]. The later FIX-HF-5C2 study supported the safety and performance of a two-lead Optimizer system, simplifying implantation by eliminating the atrial lead [18].

Meta-analytic and registry data broadly support symptomatic benefit. Trial-level meta-analysis found significant improvement in MLHFQ but less definitive effects on mortality or hospitalization over short follow-up [19]. Individual patient data meta-analysis showed consistent improvements in functional capacity and HF-related quality of life [20]. Observational registries and longer-term cohorts suggest sustained improvements in NYHA class, MLHFQ, LVEF, and hospitalization rates, with survival comparisons favoring CCM relative to predicted risk scores; however, these nonrandomized findings remain hypothesis-generating [21-24]. Echocardiographic studies also suggest global and regional systolic improvement and reverse remodeling without simply correcting dyssynchrony [25].

Patient selection is therefore central. The best-supported population is ambulatory, persistently symptomatic HF—typically NYHA class III—despite optimized medical therapy, with LVEF 25% to 45%, sinus rhythm in the original approval studies, and no indication for CRT [17,18,26]. The role in atrial fibrillation, very low LVEF, mildly reduced EF, preserved EF, CRT nonresponders, and patients with QRS 120–149 ms is under active evaluation [22,27,28]. Procedural considerations resemble transvenous pacing or ICD implantation, with attention to septal lead position, sensing, lead interactions with ICD systems, infection, venous access, and tricuspid valve burden [29]. Major evidence gaps include the absence of large blinded, adequately powered mortality trials; uncertainty about optimal daily dose and lead targeting; durability of response; cost-effectiveness across health systems; and predictors of “super-response” [24,26,30]. In current practice, CCM should be viewed as an adjunctive, symptom-directed device therapy for carefully selected patients rather than a replacement for foundational pharmacologic therapy, ICD therapy, CRT when indicated, or advanced HF evaluation.
